title: The plan is the best case.
dek: Students planned their thesis for 33.9 days and needed 55.5 - about 64% longer. Applied to my 14 days of exam studying, the real start date is nine days earlier than the plan.
whyThisIdea: Toate ideile rămase în backlog sunt marcate ca prea apropiate de articole deja publicate, așa că am adăugat una nouă, legată de momentul ăsta: mijlocul lui noiembrie, când se planifică sesiunea de iarnă. Planning fallacy are cifre verificabile (studiul Buehler, Griffin & Ross din 1994 și povestea lui Kahneman cu manualul) și se leagă de „One thing at a time, badly.”, fără să repete aritmetica de acolo.

entry.title: The plan is the best case.
entry.titleHtml: The plan is the best case.
entry.dek: Students planned their thesis for 33.9 days and needed 55.5 - about 64% longer. Applied to my 14 days of exam studying, the real start date is nine days earlier than the plan.
body: “It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter’s Law.” — Douglas Hofstadter

Have you ever asked yourself why every plan you make is on time only in your head? Today is Thursday, the 19th of November, and this week I did something very responsible: I opened the calendar and planned the studying for the winter exams. Fourteen days of work, I decided, so I can start on the 18th of December and be done by the 31st, with time to spare. It looked perfect. And then I remembered that almost every plan I have made like this looked perfect too. So the question is: is my plan a prediction, or is it just the best thing that could happen? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at has a name, and the name is older than me. Psychologists call it the planning fallacy, and it was named by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky at the end of the 1970s. The idea is simple: when we estimate how long our own task will take, we are too optimistic, even when we know that tasks like it took longer before. I did not meet it in a book first. I met it in my own calendar, in every “I will finish it this weekend” that became the next weekend.

Firstly, let’s split my title in two, the way I like to do. “The plan” and “the best case”. When I plan, I imagine the work itself - open the book, read the chapter, do the exercises, next. What I do not imagine is everything around it: the day I am sick, the friend’s birthday, the chapter that is twice as hard as the others, the evening I simply do not feel like it. None of those are in the plan, because none of them are the task. But all of them are in the real two weeks. <u>A plan is a story about the work, and real life is the work plus everything else.</u> So the plan is not the average case. It is the case where nothing else happens, and that case almost never comes.

Secondly, let’s look at the numbers, because there is a study that I think every student should know. In 1994, the psychologists Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin and Michael Ross asked psychology students who were writing their final thesis how long it would take them to finish. On average, the students said 33.9 days. On average, it took them 55.5 days. And only about 30% finished in the time they had predicted. Let’s put it in perspective:
55.5 - 33.9 = 21.6 days late
55.5 ÷ 33.9 = 1.64, so the real work took about 64% longer than the plan

Now let’s apply the same number to my own calendar, because this is where it stopped being theory for me. My plan is 14 days of studying.
14 × 1.64 = about 23 days
If I still want to be done by the 31st of December, those 23 days start on the 9th of December, not on the 18th. Nine days earlier. And this is the part that surprised me: the plan does not fail on the 31st, it fails on the 9th, on a normal Wednesday when I look at the calendar, see that I “still have time”, and do nothing. A deadline is missed long before it arrives - it is missed on the day you should have started.

Thirdly, and this is the story that made me take it seriously, because it happened to the man who named the problem. In “Thinking, Fast and Slow”, Kahneman tells how, years before, he was in a team writing a textbook for schools in Israel. One day he asked everybody to write down how long they thought it would take to finish. The answers were around two years. Then he asked Seymour Fox, the curriculum expert in the team, how long it had taken other teams like theirs. Fox thought about it for a while and then admitted that many of them never finished, and the ones that did needed seven to ten years. In his essay about it, Kahneman writes that about 40% gave up. The team continued anyway. The book was finished about eight years later, and by then nobody wanted to use it.
8 ÷ 2 = 4 times longer than the plan

What I find most interesting is not the number, it is that Fox already knew. He had the answer in his head the whole time, but when he made his own estimate, he did not use it. Kahneman calls this the difference between the inside view - looking at your own plan, your own team, your own good intentions - and the outside view - asking how long this kind of thing usually takes for people like you. The inside view asks “how long should it take?”, the outside view asks “how long did it take?”. And the second question is almost always less pleasant, and almost always more correct.

So here is what I am going to try, because I do not want this to stay only an idea. From today, next to every estimate I write in my calendar, I will write a second date - the day it was actually done. Not to feel bad about it, but to build my own outside view. After a month I will not need the 1.64 of some students from 1994, I will have my own number. And for the winter exams, I am moving the start to the 9th of December, today, while it is still easy.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe that my plans describe the best case and not the real one, and that the fix is to look backwards before I look forwards. But I have to be honest about two things. If I multiply everything by 1.64, there is a danger that the work just grows to fill the extra time - Cyril Northcote Parkinson wrote about exactly that in 1955, and I know myself well enough to be worried. And a little optimism is not only a bug. If I had known on the first day how long this blog would really take every week, maybe I would not have started it at all. What I take from it is smaller: the plan is a good place to start, but a bad place to set the deadline.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
